newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Bank of Boston Brazil unit sees growth in retail.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Boston Brazil unit sees growth in retail.

text.p: Bank of Boston Corp's Brazil unit expects 50 percent of its 1997 revenues to come from retail banking, president Carlos Craide said on Thursday.

Craide, previously an executive director of Citicorp's Citibank Brazil subsidiary, was hired to replace Henrique Meirelles, who became Bank of Boston's president and chief operating officer in the U.S early in October.
Craide told reporters that retail banking, which currently accounts for 37 percent of revenues, is the segment he believes will grow the most in 1997.

"Our retail will experience its great phase of growth as of 1997," he said, adding that retail also will be the main market niche in which the bank will compete with Citibank, where he worked for 22 years.

As for credit cards, Craide expects to raise by at least 50 percent the number of users in 1997 and reach 400,000 cards by the end of next year. The bank expects to close this year with about 200,000 cards.
Banco de Boston also plans to begin consumer financing in early 1997, offering car, truck and durable goods loans.
Craide added that he expects the bank's credit portfolio can reach $200 million next year.

Under the bank's strategy to increase retail banking, Banco de Boston has prequalified to participate in the privatization auction of Rio de Janeiro state bank Banerj, expected to take place in December.
But Craide said the bank has not yet decided whether or not it will bid on Banerj at the auction.

"We prequalified to examine the deal. We have not made any decision yet," he said, adding that the bank is considering Banerj in the case of, in a second stage of its expansion plans in retail banking, it needs a larger branch network and client portfolio.

"We will only buy a bank which adds value. It must be a bank with an interesting branch network, but also with clients and products," he said, noting the institution is not considering any other bank acquisitions.

Craide said Banco de Boston, which now has 50,000 current accounts holders and 28 branches, expects to close 1997 with 70,000 to 80,000 clients and open 10 new branches per year over the next three years.
Regarding capital markets, Craide said the bank is investing to become a big player and is particularly eyeing Brazilian privatizations in 1997.
